title: India Rebased Its GDP, but Rs 34.5 Lakh Crore of Women's Work Counts for Nothing
excerpt: A ministry-backed study values women's unpaid domestic and care work at up to Rs 34.5 lakh crore — an estimated 15-17% of GDP depending on the wage used — yet the February 2026 rebasing still leaves it outside the accounts.
body:
• India moved its GDP base year to 2022-23 in February 2026, but unpaid domestic and care work — done overwhelmingly by women — remains outside GDP's production boundary.
  • A study backed by the Ministry of Women and Child Development values that work at up to Rs 34.5 lakh crore at weighted average wages (about 17% of GDP on 2019-20 rates), and Rs 30.7 lakh crore at minimum wages — estimates, not measured output.
  • Analysis of Time Use Survey data reported by YourStory puts women's unpaid domestic and care work at 343 minutes a day against 43 minutes for men, with 93% of women doing such work compared with 44% of men.
  • Female labour-force participation has risen from 23.3% in 2017-18 to about 40% in 2025 (Periodic Labour Force Survey), but the unpaid load at home has barely moved — paid work largely adds a second shift.

In February 2026, India moved its GDP base year to 2022-23, brought in new data sources and reassessed the size of the informal economy. The economy still grew 7.8% in the quarter that followed, keeping India the fastest-growing major economy. Yet one category of work counted for nothing in that arithmetic, as YourStory reports: the unpaid domestic and care work that makes every paid job possible.

An estimate, stated precisely

The Rs 34.5 lakh crore figure is an estimate whose size depends on the wage used to value the hours. The care-economy study prepared with the support of the Ministry of Women and Child Development — Formulating a Strategy for India's Care Economy — values the hours women spend on unpaid care two ways. At minimum wages, the work is worth about Rs 30.7 lakh crore, close to 5% of GDP in 2019-20. At weighted average wages, it rises to about Rs 34.5 lakh crore, or 17% of GDP on the same wage base — a summarised range of 15% to 17% of GDP.

Those are valuation exercises, not output anyone measured — the ILO puts unpaid care at between 10% and 39% of GDP across countries, and no official Indian account currently reconciles the estimates.

Why GDP leaves it out

GDP has a defined production boundary. A creche worker paid to look after a child is economic activity; a mother or grandmother doing the same job for free is not — the value has not disappeared, only the payment has.

The time itself is measured. India's Time Use Survey 2024 shows women aged 15 to 59 spend about 201 minutes a day more than men on unpaid household work; a deeper analysis of the unit-level data reported by YourStory puts women's unpaid domestic and care work at 343 minutes a day against 43 minutes for men. The survey programme itself is published by the Ministry of Statistics — its Time Use Survey report concedes, in YourStory's quotation, that leaving out unpaid services means GDP "underestimates considerably the total income of a nation."

The second shift

On UNDP figures cited by YourStory, 44.5% of Indian women outside the labour force cite childcare and homemaking as the main reason. Participation has climbed — 23.3% in 2017-18 to about 40% in 2025 on the Periodic Labour Force Survey measure — yet the unpaid workload has barely moved in five years.

The government's own documents hold both halves of that contradiction. The Economic Survey's employment chapter calls the care economy a promising source of jobs, and the Economic Survey 2025-26 targets a 55% female workforce. But under the Palna scheme, only 11,395 anganwadi-cum-creches had been approved against a target of 17,000 by March 2025,

On the ILO's harmonised estimates, India's female labour-force participation was 32% in 2025, against 59% in China, 56.5% in Japan and 46.5% in Bangladesh.

What is being proposed

The argument is not to abandon GDP but to add a satellite account — a supplementary ledger measuring activity beyond the production boundary. India already has the raw material: two national Time Use Surveys and an accepted valuation method.

Beyond measurement, the proposals are to invest in care as infrastructure — the UNDP estimate YourStory cites holds that spending about 2% of GDP on care services could create more than 11 million jobs, a figure the ministry-backed study also reaches using ILO research — and to judge care spending by its effect on employment, not only as welfare. A working paper from the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister this year calls for moving care "from private burden to social and economic infrastructure."

For diaspora families, the same economy includes care for ageing parents in India — the ministry-backed study counts more than 120 million people over 60 among those requiring care. The open question is whether measurement, budgeting and delivery will now follow.
